idiom_name: actor-owned state machine + ContinuousClock deadline + Task.sleep transition
implementation_notes: Swift ships no first-party circuit breaker and the only long-standing package (Kitura's CircuitBreaker) targets Swift 5.1 and is no longer developed, so the realization is hand-written: an actor owns the state, counters and a ContinuousClock deadline, admit() gives callers one atomic decision, and record(_:) counts the outcome after the awaited call returns. Actor isolation removes the locking problem, the monotonic clocks make the cooldown immune to wall-clock changes, and Task.sleep can schedule the open-to-half-open transition when recovery must start even without traffic. Nothing replaces the classic structure here, so the classic form is always the choice; the design decisions are the actor boundary (one per dependency, never per call) and awaiting the network call outside the actor so the breaker does not serialize requests.
pitfalls: Actor isolation is reentrancy-safe but not atomic across awaits, so the read-modify-write of state must happen inside one synchronous actor method (admit/record) or two tasks interleave and admit more trials than configured.
ContinuousClock and SuspendingClock are the monotonic clocks; a Date() deadline moves with the wall clock and can hold the circuit open, or close it, at the wrong moment.
The guarded call must be awaited outside the actor: awaiting the network request inside an actor method serializes every request behind one and defeats the breaker.
Breaker state is process-local, so a restart immediately re-probes a dependency that may still be down; accept that or persist the trip time if the cooldown must survive restarts.
